blindSummary:
This country has an improving trajectory on trans rights and a major welcoming tourist hub (the capital), offset by unprepared detention systems and elevated baseline social hostility. Legal gender recognition no longer requires surgery — the constitutional court struck that requirement in 2024 and the ministry of health implemented the reform in 2025 — but it still requires a medical diagnosis and 6-12 months' observation (improving, not self-ID).

If detained, the system is unprepared: the supreme court in November 2025 demanded prison rules for trans people, and there is a documented case of police mishandling the extradition-detention of an HIV-positive trans foreigner. About half of LGBTIQ people report being targeted by insults, assault or threats over five years, and a far-right party uses "deviant" rhetoric; the capital and larger cities are welcoming, but harassment is more likely in rural areas or late at night.

Bathrooms are unrestricted, there is no criminalisation of trans identity, and the region's visa-free border zone poses no trans-specific friction.
blindOutOfScope: Pickpocketing and fake-plainclothes-police scams in the capital affect all tourists.
blindSourceSummaries: Constitutional court judgment (24 April 2024), legal summary: the court struck down the requirement that surgery including sterilisation be a condition for official legal sex change - a landmark ruling ending compulsory sterilisation as a condition of legal gender recognition in this country.
NOTE: not retrievable at research time (HTTP 401); the underlying newswire report (June 2025) covers this country dropping the surgery requirement for legal gender change.

Legal-news portal (March 2023): administrative courts clashed over how immigration police handle detained trans foreigners - the supreme administrative court criticised a municipal court's sarcastic moral lectures toward an HIV-positive trans detainee in transition, and ruled authorities must properly assess whether detainees are 'potentially vulnerable persons' before placement in detention facilities.

Legal-news portal (Nov 2025): this country's prisons are unprepared for trans people and lack clear rules; the supreme court demands the prison concept explicitly address the needs of people in or after transition, citing the constitutional court ruling that no longer conditions legal gender change on surgery; the human-rights commissioner supports a binding regulation while the ministry claims existing frameworks suffice.

Regional LGBTI-rights organisation's annual review 2024 (covering 2023), chapter on this country: politicians' anti-LGBT speech rose from 43% (2018) to 71% (2023); 43% of LGBT+ people reported discrimination/harassment in five years, highest among trans and non-binary respondents; a drag story-time event was disrupted in a regional city; the new asylum law includes SOGI grounds; a business pride forum published a trans-inclusive workplace toolkit.

Regional LGBTI-rights organisation's annual review 2025 (covering 2024), chapter on this country: after the constitutional court repealed the surgery requirement for legal gender recognition, the justice minister made transphobic statements (to the effect of preventing men from giving birth); a far-right party circulated anti-LGBT election leaflets; the government approved a criminal-code amendment extending hate-crime protections to sexual orientation and gender identity (pending in parliament).
A foreign government's travel advice for this country: safety and security section (terrorism threat, crime, etc.). General travel advice, not trans-specific.

Travel portal (Feb 2026): the capital and larger cities are generally welcoming for LGBTQ+ solo travellers, but harassment can occur and risk is higher in rural areas or late-night settings; practical safety tips and local resources.

Regional security organisation's 2024 hate-crime report for this country: the country regularly reports data; 94 hate crimes recorded by police in 2024, 46 prosecuted, 42 sentenced; action plans on combating extremism and prejudicial hatred introduced 2023; the organisation notes recording does not sufficiently distinguish hate crimes.

National daily with press agency (June 2018): the government supported a bill allowing same-sex marriage (46 MPs from six parties), which would replace registered partnerships; a marriage-equality fairness campaign welcomed the decision - context of the marriage-equality debate.
blindLocalsOnly: The legal-gender-recognition reform (diagnosis + observation, no surgery) is a resident-facing process; the supreme court's demand for prison rules concerns resident detainees.
